This message comes from Odoo, the all-in-one business management software platform.
Whether you're a small or large business, Odoo gives you one flexible platform built to grow with you.
Try today for free at Odoo.com/NPRPodcasts.
This is NPR News Now, the latest headlines every hour.
Live from NPR News in Washington, I'm Windsor Johnston.
The United Nations climate change talks have ended in Turkey without a broad agreement.
The European Union and several countries rejected a draft that left out any mention of coal, oil or natural gas,
the main drivers of global warming.
Ireland's climate minister, Dara O'Brien, led the EU delegation.
This is not the end of climate multilateralism.
This should actually be a reset, this should actually be a reality check that science does not lie.
And even to have to fight for science to get that in to a COP agreement just shows you the battle that we had.
But we could not, with any good conscience, support a text that effectively denies what is happening in the world
and was hijacked by fossil fuel producers.
Nearly 200 countries took part in the summit known as COP 31, the United States, was absent.
British Prime Minister Andy Burnham has made it clear his Labour Party government may consider having the UK rejoin the European Union.
But two of his predecessors are speaking out against the idea.
Vicky Barker reports from London.
The former Conservative Prime Minister Theresa May, whose own Brexit blueprint was ripped up by her successor Boris Johnson,
has accused Andy Burnham of treating Brits who voted to leave the EU as simpletons.
He wants to pat them on the head and say, you know what, remember that vote?
Well, you got it wrong, didn't you?
So have another go and come up with the right answer.
And a former Labour Prime Minister Tony Blair, who campaigned to remain, says changes for the worse within Europe since that 2016 referendum
mean the UK should only consider rejoining a reformed European Union.
For NPR News, I'm Vicky Barker in London.
The Port of Seattle is asking federal officials whether immigration agents followed airport protocol during an arrest at Seattle-Tacoma International Airport on Saturday.
Kate Stone from member station KUOW reports.
Witness video obtained by KUOW shows masked agents pulling two passengers out of the boarding line for the Los Angeles bound flight.
Security says ICE targeted Ricardo Lorondo Mendoza and arrested Sofia Hernandez Meilla, saying she threw hot coffee and will face a federal assault charge.
ICE says both are from Mexico and overstayed visas.
Passenger Aiden Mendoza, no relation, walked off the flight after watching what unfolded.
We want to help, but, you know, we're literally all trapped in this type of hallway, like we could get her as well.
Alaska Airlines and the Port of Seattle say they were not notified.
Port officials are reviewing whether DHS breached airport protocols.
For NPR News, I'm Kate Stone in Seattle.
It's NPR.
President Trump says he's ready to work with Democrats in the next Congress to cap credit card interest rates at 10 percent.
Trump had pitched the cap when he was running for reelection in 2024.
Banks and congressional Republicans showed little interest.
Democrats have backed the idea.
The median credit card rate is just over 22 percent.
Researchers estimate a 10 percent cap could save Americans $100 billion a year.
The death toll from a boating accident in Nigeria's waterways on Friday is now at least 24.
Michael Koloki has more from Nairobi.
According to authorities, the boat was ferrying passengers traveling to a funeral when it capsized at a river junction in the country's southern state of Bailasa.
Police say that the boat had suffered a mechanical failure.
Dozens of people have been rescued with some taken to local health facilities after sustaining a variety of injuries.
Boating accidents are common in Nigeria's crowded inland waterways.
Three years ago, at least 100 people died when a boat ferrying passengers on a river in the north central region of the country capsized.
For NPR News, I'm Michael Koloki in Nairobi.
A fire swept through a candy factory west of Jakarta, Indonesia on Saturday.
Officials initially reported at least three workers were killed and dozens remain unaccounted for.
Police say crews will resume the search tomorrow morning.
This is NPR News.

topics.text: UN climate talks in Turkey end without broad agreement after EU rejects draft omitting fossil fuels
Ireland's climate minister Dara O'Brien criticizes climate talks text as denying science
Former PMs Theresa May and Tony Blair criticize Andy Burnham over possible UK return to EU
Port of Seattle questions DHS over immigration arrest at Seattle-Tacoma airport
Trump says he will work with Democrats to cap credit card interest rates at 10 percent
Death toll from Nigeria boat capsizing on river rises to at least 24
Fire sweeps through candy factory west of Jakarta, Indonesia, killing at least three workers
